author: DAVID BRIGGS
title: Briggs: Verlander rocked, but Toledo shows legend the love on electric night - NewsBreak
text:
By DAVID BRIGGS ,
1 hours ago
The last time Justin Verlander pitched in Toledo, the dinosaur was the sideshow.
On a perfect June night in 2015, a then-record crowd of 13,300 poured into Fifth Third Field for a rehab start that felt like a major league exhibition. The Mud Hens wore dinosaur uniforms for a Jurassic World promotion, and somebody dressed as a giant velociraptor delivered the game ball to an amused Verlander.
It was peak minor league baseball.
On Wednesday, Verlander made his return, wearing a little gray in his beard and the Hens’ traditional home whites. The three-time Cy Young Award winner is now 43 and in the ninth inning of his Hall of Fame career.
This time, his younger brother, Ben, cracked on X …
“He’s back, and he’s the dinosaur delivering the first pitch.”
Ba-dum-tss!
No worries, though.
The 10,500 fans who packed the downtown park on a night as electric as it was roasting did not seem especially concerned with the distinction.
Or, for that matter, that Verlander got the postgame home run derby going a little early (hey, his brother started it!).
And why would they?
What mattered was that he was here.
The guy in the dinosaur costume behind the St. Paul dugout holding an "I HEART JV" sign spoke for just about everyone.
You should have heard ‘em.
As Verlander exited with two outs in the sixth after surrendering his third and fourth homers of the night, the crowd rose and delivered the loudest ovation the place has heard in years.
JV smiled later.
“Walking off after such a bad game and to have them give the ovation that they did,” he said, “it was really touching.”
Put another way, the Hens’ 12-1 loss to St. Paul was the most celebratory blowout defeat in Hens history.
No, this was not the Verlander of old — or even the one who struck out nine in his last start here.
Verlander allowed four home runs. Aaron Sabato jumped an 88-mph slider in the second, Kyle Fedko bombed one to center in the third, and the visitors added another two blasts in the sixth.
And, no, this was not the detour down I-75 that Verlander envisioned when he signed a one-year, $13 million contract to return to the Tigers.
The idea was for a feel-good homecoming that would help push a Tigers team in pursuit of a championship over the top.
Instead, he went down with left hip inflammation after one start, and the Tigers got off to a no good, very bad, horrible start, too.
But we’ll leave the bigger picture for the Tigers to sort out. (My two cents: Verlander probably belongs in the Tigers’ bullpen.)
Besides, who’s to say what happens next?
The Tigers are starting to show signs of life, and, for the record, Verlander still has some, too.
A more charitable interpretation of his night: he used the rehab start to work off the rust — three of the homers came on hanging sliders — and his arm actually looks strong. One time he did look like the Verlander of old? In the fourth inning, he pumped a 95.5-mph fastball past Ben Ross for a strikeout.
A week after throwing 64 pitches across five innings for the Hens last week in Iowa, Verlander stretched out to 89 pitches, 57 for strikes. He allowed four runs on five hits and struck out three in 5⅔ innings.
“I got my volume up and I threw six innings,” Verlander said. “Those are positives, obviously. The home runs were not great, but kept working on a pitch that they kept hitting. They kept hitting it. I kept trying to work on it in game and treat it a little bit like a spring training game, where if something isn't going well that day, you have the opportunity to try to hone it in.”
“I feel pretty good,” he added. “Today was tough, the first real humid game I've had … and that last inning I kind of felt like a wet rag, but i was able to get through it and stay healthy.
“So, check.”
For the fans, too.
If Verlander came to Toledo looking for innings, the crowd came for a memory.
Check, and check.
